front.title: MAP Identity: Agent Identifiers, Key Hierarchy, Delegation, and Lifecycle

abstract.t: Defines the self-certifying MAP agent identifier (AgentID), a three-tier key hierarchy (root, device, session), delegation certificates with attenuating caveats, key rotation and revocation records, ephemeral and organizational identities, hardware-backed keys, and interoperability with W3C DIDs (did:key, did:web), libp2p PeerIDs, and WebAuthn.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document family are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here. No adaptation or weakening of these terms applies.

section.name: Design position
section.t: Identity in MAP is a keypair, not a name, and confers nothing but attributability (arch T3–T5). There is no global PKI and no certificate authority; all authority statements are peer-issued delegations verifiable offline. The identifier is deliberately byte-compatible with two deployed ecosystems so that no bespoke resolver is needed (fixes critique C13):

section.t: MAP mandates Ed25519 identities on libp2p transports, so the transport peer identity and AgentID derive from the same key (§3.2).

section.name: Key hierarchy
section.sourcecode: Root Identity Key (RIK) — Ed25519; SHOULD be offline or hardware-backed; | signs only: delegations, rotation, revocation. v DelegationCert (scope: all or subset; long-lived) Device Key (DK) — per device/process; signs descriptors, | delegations to session keys, receipts. v DelegationCert (scope: narrow; short-lived, hours) Session Key (SK) — per session or per counterparty; used as the transport static key and envelope signer.
section.t: Single-key operation (RIK = DK = SK) is permitted for constrained or low-value agents; the hierarchy is the RECOMMENDED posture because it bounds blast radius: SK compromise burns hours, DK compromise burns one device until revoked, RIK compromise is identity loss (§7).

section.name: Format
section.sourcecode: AgentID(bytes) = multicodec-varint(key-type) || raw-public-key ed25519-pub = 0xED 0x01 || 32 bytes (suite 1/2) AgentID(text) = multibase(base58btc, AgentID(bytes)) ; "z6Mk..." DID form = "did:key:" || AgentID(text)
section.t: Future suites register their multicodec here; verifiers dispatch on the prefix — this is the identity leg of cryptographic agility.

section.name: Binding rules
section.t: B1: On libp2p, the connection's PeerID key MUST equal the peer's SK, and the envelope kid MUST be an AgentID whose key is that SK — either directly, or as the LEAF subject of a delegation chain carried in ProtHdr key 33. B2: On TLS transports, the certificate/raw public key MUST satisfy the same rule. B3: kid names the signing key; the accountable identity is the chain root's issuer when a chain is present, and kid itself otherwise. Verifiers resolve and report the accountable identity; receipts and trust records accrue to it.

section.name: Delegation certificates
section.sourcecode: DelegationCert = Envelope ; msg-type 0x0502, out-of-session DelegateBody = { ; carried in Body key 10 1 => AgentID, ; issuer (parent key) 2 => AgentID, ; subject (child key) 3 => Timestamp, ; not-before 4 => Timestamp, ; not-after ? 5 => [+ CapURI], ; capability scope (absent = all) ? 6 => [+ ZoneLabel], ; zone scope ? 7 => uint, ; max further delegation depth ? 8 => { * int => any } ; caveats (registry; e.g. budget, } ; audience, task-id pinning)
section.t: Chain validation: each cert's issuer key signs its envelope; each child is the next cert's issuer; scopes/zones/depth only ever attenuate (a child scope MUST be a subset of the parent's; violations ⇒ 2003); all validity windows MUST cover the verification time; the envelope kid MUST equal the chain LEAF's subject (the leaf key produces the envelope signature; violations ⇒ 2003), and the verifier resolves the chain root's issuer as the accountable identity (§3.2 B3). max-depth (key 7) bounds further delegation below the declaring certificate: a chain is invalid (2003) when any certificate has more certificates between itself and the leaf than its declared max-depth — a cert with max-depth 0 must itself be the leaf cert. The byte-level behavior of these rules is fixed by TV-012 and NV-009. Semantics deliberately parallel UCAN (informative reference) so existing tooling and audit intuition transfer. Tool-grant tokens in tasks §7 are DelegationCerts with task-pinning caveats — one mechanism, two uses.

Chains are carried in ProtHdr key 33, ordered leaf..root (core §6). A chain MUST NOT exceed 8 certificates (a denial-of-service bound: chain validation is one signature verification per link). An unknown caveat key MUST invalidate the entire chain (fail-closed: a caveat is a restriction, so silently ignoring one would widen scope). Registered caveat keys (§11): 1 = task-pinning (value: a 32-byte TaskID, tasks §1 — the chain is valid only for envelopes whose Body references that task; the referencing check is performed by the consumer); 2 = audience (value: a 34-byte AgentID — the chain is valid only when the validating party's own AgentID equals it).

section.name: Descriptor binding and proof of possession
section.t: An agent proves control of its AgentID implicitly: every envelope is signed, and sessions are channel-bound (core §7.3). No separate challenge-response registration exists or is needed; a DHT record or descriptor is trusted exactly as far as its signature chain.

section.name: Organizational and ephemeral identities
section.t: Organizational: an org RIK delegates to member DKs with scoped caveats; counterparties see receipts accrue to the org AgentID while members remain individually revocable. Orgs MAY additionally publish did:web documents listing their AgentID(s) to anchor a human-meaningful name; MAP itself never requires the DNS anchor (G1) and treats it as evidence, not authority.

Ephemeral (Zone 3 / anonymous): a fresh keypair with no delegation chain. Fully permitted (arch G4). Ephemeral identities start with zero evidence, are subject to admission costs where the mesh applies them (trust §5), and cannot benefit from any prior reputation — which is precisely the Sybil containment property. Linkability trade-off is the user's: reuse accrues evidence; rotation buys privacy.

section.name: Rotation and revocation
section.t: ROTATE MUST be signed by the old key (proving continuity) and SHOULD be countersigned by the new key (an ext field carries the second signature) proving possession. REVOKE is signed by the revoked key's parent (for DK/SK) or by the RIK itself (self-revocation on compromise; reason 1). Distribution: rotation/revocation records are stored in the DHT under H("map:id:" || AgentID) and gossiped on a low-rate identity topic; verifiers of high-value operations SHOULD fetch freshness ≤24 h old and MUST treat known-revoked keys as 2002. There is no global instant revocation (T8); risk-tier your checks. RIK compromise is unrecoverable by design — evidence and receipts attach to keys, not names; this is stated plainly rather than papered over.

section.name: Hardware backing and WebAuthn
section.t: RIKs and DKs SHOULD reside in hardware (TPM 2.0, secure enclave, YubiKey/ CTAP2 authenticators). WebAuthn interop: an authenticator-resident Ed25519 credential (COSE alg -8) can serve directly as a RIK; the WebAuthn assertion format is not carried on the wire — the authenticator simply performs the RIK's rare signatures (delegations, rotations). Attestation of hardware residence MAY be advertised in the descriptor SecurityProfile (discovery §5) and lifts trust priors per local policy only.

section.name: Validation summary (normative checklist)
section.t: On any signed object: resolve kid → root AgentID; validate delegation chain per §4 (scope, zone, depth, time); check revocation state per local freshness policy; verify signature over received bytes (core I1); verify transport binding B1–B3 for in-session messages. Errors: 2000–2005.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Key hierarchy limits blast radius but adds chain-validation surface — implementations MUST cap chain length (default 5) and total cert bytes. Rotation records signed only by old keys allow an attacker holding a stolen key to rotate away from the victim; hence the countersignature requirement and grace period during which both keys' signatures are accepted and either MAY REVOKE (reason 1) — a compromise observed during grace is recoverable. Timestamp trust follows core §14. Privacy: delegation chains reveal organizational structure; Zone-2/3 interactions SHOULD present minimal chains (leaf + one parent).

section.name: IANA-Style Considerations
section.t: Registries established: MAP Key Types (multicodec bindings); MAP Delegation Caveats; MAP Revocation Reasons. The assigned values and the family-wide index are in draft-map-wire-01.md §3.7, §3.8, and §3.9; in case of divergence the normative tables in §4 govern.
